newsitem.title: USA: Arizona governor angrily denies extortion charge.
newsitem.headline: Arizona governor angrily denies extortion charge.

text.p: Arizona Gov. Fife Symington angrily denied Friday he used the power of his office in a desperate attempt to extort loan concessions from union pension funds for a downtown Phoenix shopping centre.
In fiery testimony, the Republican governor said he never threatened to flex his political muscle against pension advisers by saying he would ruin the project if his demands were not met.

Symington, facing a barrage of questions from lead prosecutor David Schindler, said discussions about releasing him from a $10 million personal guarantee and changing loan payments were at the heart of the 1991 meeting in the governor's office at the state Capitol.
The meeting occurred just months after the two-term governor was elected to office for the first time.

With the words "I never said that," Symington rejected claims that he told the advisers he would make sure state-financed Arizona State University would not renew its lease if lenders threw the project into default. The university is the center's largest tenant.
He also called untrue allegations that he pledged to dissuade Maricopa County and Arizona Democratic Representative Ed Pastor from leasing space at the troubled centre.
The attempted extortion charge is one of the most explosive being leveled against Symington in an sweeping indictment.
Symington faces 21 other counts of federal fraud and perjury and would be ousted from office if convicted on even a single count. He also could be sentenced to prison.
Schindler hammered away at Symington during day-long cross-examination, using the notes of pension fund officials to try to prove that the extortion allegations were real.
The notes painted a picture of an angry man who was pressing to escape his personal guarantee at a time when he was deeply in debt.
"It's hard to honour a personal guarantee when you're $22 million under water," he told the jury.
The prosecution also got Symington to acknowledge that any default would have been "politically embarrassing" if it became public.
But a well-prepared Symington charged that the notes were "full of errors" and that there was nothing criminal about his behaviour at the time.
"I know what I did and did not do," he said.
Symington deflected assertions that he had presented lenders with an inaccurately rosy picture of his finances up to the time he sought the loan concessions.
He eventually filed Chapter 7 bankruptcy in September 1995, awash in a sea of debt and facing an $11 million judgment against him won by the union pension funds.
The perjury count stems from statements he made during bankruptcy proceedings. He denied Friday that he had lied.

The day's proceedings were a marked departure from the trial's previous document-by-document dissection of the financial information he submitted to lenders as a developer in the mid-1980s through the early 1990s.

Prosecutors claim he deliberately lied to lenders to save his crumbling real estate empire. They contend he made the false statements to various financial institutions, telling lenders different stories depending on whether he sought money for projects or relief from his commitments.
Symington maintains that he made mistakes but did not intentionally defraud the variety of financial institutions he dealt with during his days as a developer.
He said the institutions were well aware of his financial condition and never questioned his filings.
Symington is the last defence witness and is expected to wrap up his testimony Tuesday. The jury is expected to get the case Thursday.
